strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction: global attention becomes dominant as the number of views grows, so an inference-only retrofit has clear potential value.
The method is lightweight and training-free, preserves dense interactions involving camera/register tokens, and is demonstrated on two strong but architecturally distinct backbones, VGGT and π3.

Evaluation is broad across relative-pose, trajectory, pointmap, and scene-scale pose benchmarks. The supplementary material provides full sparsity sweeps rather than reporting only a favorable operating point.

The large-scene experiments establish meaningful speedups at useful accuracy levels. For example, at 200 frames, the S25 variants retain close pose performance while reducing VGGT runtime from 18.0 s to 8.5 s and π3 runtime from 13.9 s to 6.8 s.

Ablations support the decision to keep special-token interactions dense and show that learned mask projections provide little benefit over the simpler training-free predictor. The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The headline combination of “up to 4× faster” and “comparable task performance” is not fully supported by the same operating point. Near-4× acceleration occurs at S75, where pose accuracy collapses substantially: for 200-frame VGGT, RRA@5 drops from 83.9 to 57.1 and RTA@5 from 79.9 to 60.8. Accuracy-preserving S25 settings provide closer to 2× speedup on long sequences. This claim should be qualified, and Pareto operating points should be stated explicitly.

The attention-analysis evidence is weaker than claimed. Small mean softmax entries are inevitable for very long sequences, while maxima and a few selected qualitative matches do not establish that most probability mass is sparse or geometrically correct. Quantitative top-k mass/entropy statistics and correspondence or epipolar-error evaluation are absent. The downstream sparsification results demonstrate redundancy, but not the stronger interpretation as exhaustive geometric matching.

The technical novelty is limited: the core mechanism is pooled query-key similarity followed by CDF/top-k block selection, closely related to SpargeAttention. Treating a small set of special tokens densely is sensible and useful, but incremental. There is no controlled comparison against the complete SpargeAttention method, alternative sparse-attention retrofits, or even the layer-skipping strategy suggested by the paper’s own analysis.

The formal definition in Eq. (2) is technically incorrect as written: multiplying logits by a binary mask before softmax sets excluded logits to zero rather than negative infinity, so they still receive probability mass. Presumably the implemented block-sparse kernel performs true masking, but the discrepancy leaves the mathematical method ambiguous.

The definition of “sparsity ratio” is internally inconsistent. Section 5 calls it the fraction of computed entries, whereas the stated speedup 1/(1−x), labels such as S75, and reported results treat it as the fraction skipped. This affects interpretation of the main trade-off and is more than a cosmetic notation issue.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete for a systems-oriented contribution. Timing is reported only on one H100 GPU, without variance, warm-up/repetition protocol, precision, kernel version, or peak-memory measurements. Sparse execution is sometimes slower for 25 frames, but the crossover point and mask-construction overhead are not analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited by missing main-method details, including the actual query/key block sizes, whether masks are selected per head, exact block-ranking scope, sparse-kernel configuration, and timing setup. These omissions make faithful reproduction difficult despite the conceptually simple algorithm.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/827df8341e73405c8da026dadd4558ab/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a real scalability bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction: global attention becomes dominant as the number of input views grows.
The training-free retrofit is practically attractive and is evaluated on both VGGT and π3, suggesting that the approach is not tied to one checkpoint or architecture.

The evaluation covers pose estimation and point-map reconstruction across several established datasets. Moderate sparsification generally causes only gradual degradation, and the Tanks & Temples experiments explicitly test scaling from 25 frames to full sequences.

The special-token ablation supports computing camera/register-token interactions densely, while the negative result for learned projections usefully shows that additional training is unnecessary in the tested setting.
The paper is clearly organized and provides extensive supplementary result tables and readable qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The principal technical contribution is insufficiently differentiated from SpargeAttention. Average-pooled query/key block scoring followed by probability-mass and top-k selection is largely an application of an existing sparse-attention recipe; the main domain-specific change is retaining dense interactions involving special tokens. There is no controlled comparison against unmodified SpargeAttention, simpler fixed/block-local masks, random or magnitude-based block selection, or the layer-skipping strategy motivated by the paper's own analysis. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which claimed innovation produces the gains.

The headline claim of 'up to 4× faster inference with comparable task performance' is not supported by a single demonstrated operating point. On full Tanks & Temples sequences, VGGT-S75 reduces runtime from 35.0 s to 10.4 s (3.37×), but RRA@5 falls from 73.4 to 46.0 and RTA@5 from 72.5 to 53.0. For π3, 27.9 s to 7.8 s (3.58×) accompanies RRA@5 dropping from 75.8 to 50.0. Settings with relatively small accuracy losses, such as S25, provide roughly 2× speedups on full sequences. Thus the best speed and comparable-accuracy results are obtained at different settings, and no reported result reaches 4× end-to-end speedup.

The attention analysis does not rigorously establish the claimed sparsity or geometric-matching interpretation. Post-softmax attention is mathematically dense; plots of maximum and average entries are not sparsity measures, and row-wise softmax constrains the overall mean. Entropy, cumulative top-k mass, effective support size, head-wise statistics, and results across scenes would be needed. A few selected correspondence visualizations are suggestive but cannot establish that the retained blocks reliably encode geometric matches. Layer-drop sensitivity demonstrates that middle layers are important, not that their attention is safely sparsifiable.

Equation (2) is technically incorrect as written: multiplying logits by a binary mask before softmax sets excluded logits to zero rather than assigning them negative infinity, so excluded entries still receive probability mass. If this is only a notation error, the actual masked-softmax computation must be specified; as presented, the equation does not implement sparse attention.

The exposition is internally inconsistent about sparsity: Section 5 defines the sparsity ratio as the fraction of computed entries, whereas the speedup formula 1/(1−x), labels such as S75, and reported tables treat it as the fraction omitted. This ambiguity affects the interpretation and reproduction of all trade-off results.

Reproducibility of the efficiency claims is weak. The paper does not adequately specify the inference block sizes for the main method, whether masks are selected per head, boundary-block handling, exact kernel configuration, timing protocol, warm-up and repetition counts, variance, batch size, or memory consumption. Only one GPU is timed, and the accuracy tables provide no uncertainty across scene/frame sampling.

The external baselines in Figure 7 are accuracy-only values rather than hardware-controlled speed–accuracy comparisons. Therefore they show that the sparsified pretrained backbones can remain accurate, but they do not establish a better efficiency frontier than competing reconstruction or acceleration methods. Overall, the work has practical merit, but limited originality, overclaimed headline evidence, and unresolved technical/reproducibility issues make the current balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear practical bottleneck in VGGT-style multi-view reconstruction: global attention increasingly dominates runtime as the number of frames grows. Retrofitting pretrained models without backbone retraining is useful and directly relevant to scalable 3D vision.

The empirical scope is strong. The method is tested on both VGGT and π3 across relative-pose, trajectory, and pointmap benchmarks, followed by scene-level Tanks & Temples experiments spanning 25, 50, 100, 200, and full-length sequences. This breadth supports the claim that the approach generalizes across models, tasks, and sequence lengths.

The moderate-sparsity operating points provide a meaningful accuracy-efficiency trade-off. For example, on full-length Tanks & Temples, VGGT-S25 reduces runtime from 35.0 s to 17.9 s while RRA@5 changes only from 73.4 to 72.7; π3-S25 reduces 27.9 s to 13.6 s while RRA@5 changes from 75.8 to 74.8. The S50 variants still achieve roughly 2.4× speedups with modest, though non-negligible, accuracy loss.

The analysis is useful rather than purely engineering-driven: attention-map inspection, layer-drop experiments, and the special-token ablation collectively motivate where sparsification is appropriate. In particular, preserving dense interactions involving camera/register tokens is empirically shown to matter at high sparsity.

The ablation comparing training-free masks with learned linear projections is informative: the learned alternative brings little improvement, supporting the simpler training-free design. The accuracy-versus-sparsity curves also expose failure at aggressive settings rather than hiding the trade-off.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and supplemented with extensive numerical tables. Its practical contribution is potentially valuable even though it is an adaptation of existing sparse-attention ideas rather than a new reconstruction architecture.
weaknesses: The headline claim of “up to 4× faster inference with comparable task performance” overstates what is demonstrated at a single operating point. The near-4× settings incur severe degradation: on full-length Tanks & Temples, VGGT-S75 is about 3.4× faster but RRA@5 falls from 73.4 to 46.0, while π3-S75 is about 3.6× faster but falls from 75.8 to 50.0. The settings with genuinely comparable accuracy provide closer to 2× speedups; the paper should separate maximum speedup from quality-preserving speedup.

Originality is moderate. The core mechanism—pooling queries and keys, selecting important blocks, and invoking block-sparse kernels—is closely related to SpargeAttention and prior sparse-attention work. Applying and simplifying it for VGGT/π3, including special-token handling, is useful, but the paper lacks direct runtime/accuracy comparisons against the complete SpargeAttention method or other adaptive sparse-attention alternatives. Consequently, it does not isolate the benefit of the proposed selection rule from that of adopting block-sparse attention generally.

The proposed interpretation of high attention values as geometric correspondences is supported primarily by qualitative examples. No quantitative correspondence evaluation, comparison to ground-truth matches, or analysis across heads/scenes establishes how reliably attention represents geometry. Likewise, layer-drop sensitivity shows that middle layers are important, but does not by itself prove that they perform the claimed exhaustive correspondence search.

The technical description contains inconsistencies. Section 5 defines sparsity as the ratio of computed entries to total entries, but the equations, tables, and claimed speedup 1/(1−x) treat it as the fraction omitted. More importantly, Eq. (2) writes softmax((QKᵀ)⊙M), which does not mask excluded entries because zero logits retain nonzero softmax probability; a correct formulation requires an additive −∞ mask or an explicitly restricted softmax. These appear correctable, but currently undermine precision.

Efficiency evidence is concentrated on one H100 GPU and Tanks & Temples. The manuscript omits memory measurements, isolated selector/kernel overhead, warm-up and repetition protocol, variance, and results on other hardware or sequence/resolution regimes. At 25 frames, sparse variants can even be slower, so a clearer crossover analysis is important for practical deployment.

Reproducibility is incomplete: inference block sizes and several implementation details of mask construction/kernel integration are not clearly consolidated; timing precision, compilation settings, and software configuration are not reported; and evaluations using random frame sampling provide no seeds or uncertainty estimates. These are meaningful omissions for a systems-oriented contribution, although they appear remediable rather than fundamental.

strengths: The paper addresses a real scalability bottleneck in global-attention multi-view geometry models and proposes a practical, training-free block-sparse replacement that can be applied to pretrained systems.

Evaluation is unusually broad: the method is tested on VGGT, π3, and MapAnything across relative-pose, trajectory, and point-map benchmarks, including sequences of up to 1,000 frames. Results consistently show useful accuracy-efficiency trade-offs rather than relying on a single favorable dataset.

The experiments support the central practical result: moderate effective sparsity generally preserves most baseline accuracy, while long-sequence inference reaches roughly 2× speedup near 60% sparsity and up to about 3× at more aggressive settings.

Ablations are relevant and informative. Random masking performs substantially worse; retaining dense interactions involving special tokens is important; combining top-k and CDF selection is more robust than CDF alone; and learned mask projections provide little benefit over the training-free formulation.

The method is simple and potentially useful in practice. Separating mask prediction from the sparse-attention kernel and demonstrating transfer across three architectures strengthens the contribution despite its incremental algorithmic nature.
weaknesses: The headline claim of more than 3× acceleration while maintaining comparable performance is somewhat overstated. The clearest near-lossless operating point is around 2×, whereas speedups approaching or exceeding 3× occur mainly on very long sequences at aggressive sparsity, where VGGT and π3 can show noticeable trajectory-error degradation. The paper should distinguish these operating points more precisely.

The scientific interpretation of attention as sparse geometric correspondence is under-supported. Visual examples are suggestive, but no quantitative comparison to ground-truth correspondences, top-k attention-mass coverage, or correspondence precision is provided. Moreover, large maximum activations and small average post-softmax values do not by themselves establish sparsity, and the layer-drop study demonstrates layer importance rather than the claimed correspondence mechanism.

The method is technically close to SpargeAttention: it reuses its optimized kernel and modifies block selection by combining top-k and CDF criteria while treating special tokens densely. This is a sensible adaptation, but the conceptual novelty is modest, and the comparison does not fully isolate the speed contribution of each change relative to an equivalently tuned SpargeAttention implementation.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete for a systems-oriented contribution. Measurements are limited to an H100, absolute latency and peak-memory tables are absent, and the timing protocol, precision, warm-up/repetition procedure, and mask-construction overhead are not documented adequately. MapAnything timing is explicitly described as inaccurate. These issues limit reproducibility and confidence in portability to other GPUs.

Notation for sparsity is inconsistent and should be corrected: the main method uses ρ as the fraction skipped, while the supplement describes the dense model as ρ=1 and states that computation is reduced by factor ρ, which conflicts with the block-selection equation, speedup table, and reported effective sparsity. This appears readily correctable but currently obscures the theoretical analysis.

The manuscript does not provide a clear code-release statement or enough low-level implementation detail to reproduce the optimized result independently, including definitive block sizes for all main experiments and exact handling of dense special-token interactions within the sparse kernel.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck: global attention becomes dominant as multi-view geometry transformers process larger image collections.

The training-free block-selection mechanism is simple and potentially useful. Preserving dense interactions involving camera/register tokens is a sensible architecture-aware design choice, and the corresponding ablation shows that it materially improves robustness at high sparsity.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering three distinct models (VGGT, π3, and MapAnything), multiple pose and point-map benchmarks, and sequences of up to 1,000 frames. Results consistently show a useful accuracy-efficiency trade-off, particularly around moderate sparsity.

Comparisons against random masking, SpargeAttention variants, and learned projections provide some evidence that the proposed top-k plus CDF selection is preferable in this setting. The manuscript is generally clear and includes extensive supplementary tables.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The work largely adapts SpargeAttention's pooled-query/key block scoring and block-sparse kernel to existing geometry transformers, while omitting several SpargeAttention components and combining two standard selection rules. The paper does not clearly establish that this constitutes a substantial methodological advance beyond a useful domain-specific engineering adaptation.

The headline claim of more than 3× acceleration while maintaining comparable performance is not adequately supported. The long-sequence plots indicate roughly 2× speedup near 60% sparsity, where degradation is relatively small; speedups above 3× occur mainly at higher sparsity, where accuracy degradation is appreciable. For example, on 1,000-frame ScanNet, VGGT ATE rises from about 0.204 at low sparsity to roughly 0.277–0.284 at the configurations approaching the largest speedups, while π3 rises from 0.150 to about 0.179–0.180. MapAnything timing is explicitly described as inaccurate.

The runtime evaluation lacks the rigor expected for a systems-oriented contribution. It provides plots but no detailed absolute latency, memory usage, kernel-level breakdown, measurement variance, warm-up/repetition protocol, or comparison across hardware. Dense attention is also not included as an explicit zero-sparsity row in the supplementary result tables. These omissions make the practical advantage and reproducibility difficult to assess.

The theoretical presentation contains consequential inconsistencies. The supplement first states that dense attention corresponds to ρ=1, while Eq. (4), Eq. (7), the tables, and the surrounding discussion use ρ as the fraction skipped, so dense attention corresponds to ρ=0. Equation (6) also omits the stated number of global blocks L_G, making the displayed total-FLOP expression inconsistent with the architecture and reported speedup calculation.

Equation (2) is not a correct mathematical definition of masked sparse attention: multiplying logits by a binary mask sets excluded logits to zero rather than negative infinity, so excluded entries still receive softmax probability. The manuscript also does not precisely explain how separately computed patch-patch and special-token interactions are combined under a shared softmax normalization. These may be notation or exposition errors, but they affect the formal specification of the central method.

The claimed geometric interpretation of sparse attention is supported mainly by selected visualizations. There is no quantitative evaluation against image correspondences, epipolar consistency, or visibility, so the conclusion that high-attention entries represent geometric matching remains suggestive rather than demonstrated. Likewise, the layer-drop experiment shows layer sensitivity but does not directly validate the proposed block-selection rule.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including the block sizes used for the main training-free experiments and enough information to reproduce the timing setup and sparse kernel integration. No code or release commitment is identified in the manuscript. Overall, the method appears practically promising, but the limited originality, overstated headline claim, internally inconsistent analysis, and incomplete efficiency evidence currently make the balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important bottleneck: global attention becomes the dominant cost as the number of views grows in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models.

The proposed training-free block selection is technically sensible: pooled query-key similarities approximate block importance, combined CDF/top-k selection prevents excessively aggressive pruning, and dense handling of camera/register-token interactions is well motivated and ablated.

The empirical scope is strong. The method is tested on three architectures (VGGT, π3, and MapAnything), multiple pose and point-map benchmarks, and sequences reaching 1,000 frames. Across these settings, roughly 50–60% effective sparsity generally causes limited degradation, while longer sequences obtain about 2–3× end-to-end acceleration.

Ablations provide useful supporting evidence: random masking performs substantially worse, preserving special-token interactions matters at high sparsity, learned projections do not improve over the training-free selector, and layer-dropping experiments illuminate where global attention is most important.
The work is clearly written, includes extensive supplementary tables and qualitative results, and offers an immediately useful way to scale strong pretrained geometry models without retraining.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. The central mechanism is an adaptation and simplification of existing block-sparse attention, particularly SpargeAttention, with the main innovations being combined top-k/CDF selection and special-token handling for multi-view geometry.

The comparison labeled as SpargeAttention omits its Hilbert permutation and apparently other components. Consequently, the evidence supports superiority over the evaluated ablation, but not necessarily over a fully configured implementation of the prior method.

The strongest efficiency claim is incompletely characterized. Runtime is reported primarily through plots on one H100 GPU, without comprehensive absolute latency, peak-memory, selector-overhead, or multi-hardware measurements. MapAnything timings are explicitly described as inaccurate because of preprocessing and postprocessing.

The claim that sparse activations correspond to geometric matches is supported mostly by selected visualizations. Quantitative correspondence accuracy, attention-mass coverage, or mask-recall measurements would better substantiate this interpretation and directly validate the block selector.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for an efficiency paper: the principal block sizes and several kernel/configuration details are not clearly specified for all reported experiments, dense-baseline values are not consistently included in the full tables, and no variance or repeated-run uncertainty is reported.

The terminology around effective sparsity is briefly inconsistent: it is described as the ratio of computed entries to total entries, whereas the equations, plots, and speedup discussion treat sparsity as the skipped fraction. This appears correctable but can cause implementation ambiguity.
